differences.title: 1. PRIMARY JOB
differences.leftDesc: Prettier focuses on deterministic code formatting. It parses source into an AST, applies printer rules (line wrapping, quotes, semicolons), and emits consistent output regardless of developer preferences.
differences.rightDesc: ESLint primarily detects problems via configurable rules. It parses code into an AST, runs rule visitors on nodes, and reports issues like bugs, suspicious patterns, and style violations you define.

differences.title: 2. CONFIG MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Prettier uses a small set of options and a stable formatting algorithm. Even when options exist, the goal is “format the whole file consistently,” minimizing configuration complexity and drift across teams.
differences.rightDesc: ESLint’s configuration is rule-centric: you enable/disable rules, tune severity, and compose configs (shareable configs, plugins). Teams can encode project-specific constraints and security/business logic.

differences.title: 3. UNDER THE HOOD
differences.leftDesc: Prettier’s printer generates output by using “doc” structures representing layout decisions. It computes groups/lines/breaks to satisfy formatting width, then prints using those constraints.
differences.rightDesc: ESLint builds an AST and then executes rules that register listeners for node types. Rules can also request scope information, enabling checks that depend on bindings and control-flow context.

differences.title: 4. SCOPE & CONTEXT
differences.leftDesc: Prettier’s output decisions are largely syntactic: spacing, indentation, and formatting of constructs. It avoids deep program analysis so formatting stays fast and predictable.
differences.rightDesc: ESLint can do semantic linting when configured with parser options (and TypeScript support). Rules can understand types/scopes (e.g., no-unused-vars, no-undef, unsafe patterns) rather than pure formatting.

differences.title: 5. AUTO-FIX CAPABILITIES
differences.leftDesc: Prettier can auto-fix by re-printing files to its canonical format. The fixes are global and consistent, but it won’t generally rewrite code intent beyond layout changes.
differences.rightDesc: ESLint auto-fixes per-rule when a rule supplies a fixer function. This can include refactors like adjusting imports, removing unused code, or rewriting expressions—depending on rule authorship.

differences.title: 6. PERFORMANCE PROFILE
differences.leftDesc: Prettier is designed for consistent speed: it parses and prints, usually running as a single formatting pipeline. Work scales mostly with file size, not with rule count.
differences.rightDesc: ESLint performance depends on enabled rules and plugins. Each rule’s traversal and optional scope/type analysis adds overhead, so large rule sets can significantly increase runtime in CI.

differences.title: 7. BEST PRACTICE COMBINATION
differences.leftDesc: Teams often run Prettier as the source of truth for formatting, ensuring minimal diff noise. Keeping it separate avoids conflicts with rule-based formatting opinions and produces stable commits.
differences.rightDesc: ESLint is commonly layered with Prettier integration (e.g., disable conflicting formatting rules). Use ESLint for correctness/security and enforce architectural conventions via targeted custom rules.
